1394.title: Stilling the mind
1394.hook: yoga is the stilling of the mind's movements (Yoga Sutras 1.2)
1394.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras learn sutra 1.2 as the definition of yoga and practice stilling the mind in seated meditation, coming back again and again, with non-attachment to whatever pulls them away.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ashtanga: Patanjali's eight limbs, starting with how you treat people. Your line was eight limbs.

The Yoga Sutras don't warm up. The first line is barely a sentence: now, the teaching of yoga. The second line is the definition, and the whole book hangs on it. No poses. No breath. No gods, yet. Just a claim about what's going on behind your eyes, all day: the mind is moving. It flickers from a memory to a worry to a plan, to a song from a commercial, to the memory again. Yoga, the second line says, is what happens when that stills.
screen: `LINE ONE: NOW, THE TEACHING OF YOGA.` → `LINE TWO: THE DEFINITION.` → `THE MIND IS MOVING.`

segments.voice: Sutra one point two: yogash chitta vritti nirodhah. Yoga is the stilling of the movements of the mind. Translators reach for different English. Chitta is the mind, or the whole field of awareness. Vritti has been put as movements, fluctuations, modifications, whirls; nirodha as restraint, cessation, stilling. Then the next line: when that happens, the seer rests in its own nature. Otherwise, the line after says, the seer takes on the shape of the movements: angry when the anger moves, anxious when the worry moves. Here's the surprising part. The book lists the kinds of movement, and there are five: right knowledge, error, imagination, sleep and memory. Right knowledge is on the list. So is sleep. The stilling isn't only about clearing out bad thoughts. Even true thoughts are movements. So how does it happen? Sutra one point twelve answers in two words: practice, and non-attachment. Practice is coming back. Non-attachment is letting go of what pulls you away. And practice becomes firm, the book adds, when it's kept up for a long time, without a break, and with care. One image teachers reach for is a lake. When the wind drops, the surface goes flat, and you can see straight down to the bottom. The water was always clear. It was just moving.
screen: `THE STILLING OF THE MIND'S MOVEMENTS.` · `THE SEER RESTS IN ITS OWN NATURE.` · `FIVE MOVEMENTS, EVEN SLEEP.` · `PRACTICE, AND LETTING GO.` · then, large: `THE WATER WAS ALWAYS CLEAR.`

segments.voice: Choose a position you can hold without fidgeting, decide not to move until the bell, and let the body be the first thing that stills. Then watch the mind move, a memory, a plan, a sound, without chasing or fighting any of it. Each time you notice you've been carried off, that's the practice: come back to sitting still.
Stilling the mind. Patanjali's definition of yoga: the movements of the mind grow still, and the seer rests in its own nature. Today's word.
Your line: stilling. Wind over the water, and then the water settles. Go gently.

1395.title: Mantra repetition
1395.hook: repeating a sacred name or mantra, often on beads
1395.howItsDone: Hindus who practice japa repeat a mantra or a name of God such as Ram or Om namah Shivaya, often counting on a mala of beads, aloud, in a whisper, or silently.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was stilling the mind: Patanjali's definition of yoga, the mind's movements growing still. Your line was stilling.

A string of wooden beads hangs on a hook by a kitchen door, one spot worn smooth. Early, before the kettle, a hand takes it down. A thumb pulls one bead toward the palm. Lips move. A name is said, barely above a breath. Next bead. Same name. No new words are added. Nothing is asked for. The kettle boils and is ignored for a moment longer. Yesterday the mind was a lake, moving in the wind. Today, a way of giving it one place to move.
screen: `BEADS BY THE KITCHEN DOOR.` → `ONE BEAD, ONE NAME.` → `NOTHING ADDED, NOTHING ASKED.`

segments.voice: That's japa: the repetition of a sacred name or a mantra, said aloud, whispered, or held silently. You met the mantra back on day one hundred two, a word carried on the breath. Different Hindu communities repeat different names. Devotees of Shiva may repeat Om namah Shivaya; devotees of Rama, the name Ram. It's often counted on a string of beads called a mala, so the hand keeps the count and the mind doesn't have to. And it turns up in yesterday's book. In the Yoga Sutras, sutra one point twenty-seven says the word that expresses the Lord is the pranava, the sacred syllable Om. The next sutra gives the practice in two parts: its repetition, japa, and dwelling on its meaning. Not sound alone, not meaning alone: the word, said again and again, with attention on what it points to. From that, the following sutra says, comes turning inward, and the clearing of what stands in the way. The Bhagavad Gita goes further. There Krishna names, kind by kind, what he is among things, and among the forms of sacrifice, he says, he is japa, the sacrifice of repetition. A sacrifice that needs no fire, no food, no money. Only breath and a name. So japa isn't saying a word until it means nothing. In this picture the word is said so often that the mind, which moves all day, gets worn into one groove, like the smooth spot on the bead.
screen: `A SACRED NAME, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `BEADS KEEP THE COUNT.` · `REPETITION, AND ITS MEANING.` · `THE SACRIFICE OF REPETITION.` · then, large: `ONE GROOVE, LIKE THE SMOOTH BEAD.`

segments.voice: Choose one word and keep it: if you pray, a name from your own tradition, and if you don't, a plain word like peace, or here. Say it softly or inside twenty-seven times, three rounds of nine on your fingers, letting a little of the meaning come with each one. When you lose count, don't start over in frustration; just go on from where you think you were.
Japa. The repetition of a sacred name or mantra, often counted on beads, aloud, whispered or silent, with attention on its meaning. Today's word.

1396.title: Singing the names
1396.howItsDone: Hindu devotees gather for kirtan in temples and homes, where a leader sings a line of divine names and the group sings it back, often with harmonium, hand cymbals and drum, the pace building as it goes.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was japa: one sacred name, repeated bead by bead, with its meaning. Your line was japa.

A harmonium wheezes into a chord. Someone at the front, cross-legged on a rug, sings a short line: a name, a melody, maybe five seconds long. Then stops. And the whole room sings it back: kids, grandparents, a teenager who looks like he'd rather be elsewhere and sings anyway. The leader sings the line again, a little different. The room answers again. Hand cymbals pick up a beat. A drum joins. The lines get shorter, the answers come faster, and after a while nobody is quite sure who's leading whom.
screen: `A HARMONIUM, A LINE, A PAUSE.` → `THE ROOM SINGS IT BACK.` → `FASTER, UNTIL NOBODY LEADS.`

segments.voice: That's kirtan: singing the names and glories of God, and the kind in today's lesson is call and response. One voice calls; the many respond. Kirtan belongs to bhakti, the path of loving devotion. In the Bhagavata Purana, a boy named Prahlada, devoted to Vishnu even when his own father turns against him, lists the ways of devotion. Hearing about God comes first. Singing comes second. Remembering, third. You hear, then you sing what you heard, then it stays with you. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes great souls who are always singing his glory, striving, firm in their vows, bowing to him in devotion. Always singing, not only on holidays. Tradition remembers the Bengali saint Chaitanya leading crowds in kirtan through the streets, and the names sung today include Rama and Krishna, Shiva and the Goddess, depending on who's singing. Now look at the design. Call and response asks nothing of you but to listen and give back. You don't need the words in advance or a trained voice. You need ears and the nerve to open your mouth. The leader does the remembering; you do the answering. And then the answering does something japa can't. You hear the person next to you. Your voice is one strand in a rope. Yesterday's name, said alone, wore one groove into one mind. Today's, sung back and forth, runs through a whole room.
screen: `ONE VOICE CALLS, THE MANY RESPOND.` · `HEAR, THEN SING, THEN REMEMBER.` · `ALWAYS SINGING HIS GLORY.` · `NO TRAINED VOICE REQUIRED.` · then, large: `ONE STRAND IN A ROPE.`

segments.voice: Pick one short line: if you pray, a name you hold sacred, and if not, a simple tune of a few notes. Hum it once as the caller, then hum it back as the room, caller and room in turn. Let the answer be a little softer, or a little fuller, than the call.
Kirtan. Singing the names and glories of God, one voice calling and the many answering, a practice of Hindu bhakti. Today's word.
Your line: call and response. One voice, then the whole room. That's today, done.

1397.title: Who am I?
1397.hook: Ramana Maharshi taught self-enquiry: ask "who am I?" and trace the "I" to its source
1397.howItsDone: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-enquiry by meeting each thought with the question "to whom did this come?" and turning attention back to the sense of I, in sitting practice and through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was kirtan: one voice calls, the room answers, singing the names. Your line was call and response.

A clinic intake form asks who you are, in pieces. Name. Address. Occupation. Emergency contact. Allergies. Each box is small, and each answer is true. Fill them all in and you've described a person well enough to be treated, billed and called back. In South India, at the foot of a hill called Arunachala, a quiet teacher named Ramana Maharshi asked the same question with no boxes at all. He didn't want it filled in. He wanted it followed, the way you'd follow a stream uphill to see where it starts.
screen: `AN INTAKE FORM, IN PIECES.` → `A HILL CALLED ARUNACHALA.` → `FOLLOWED, NOT FILLED IN.`

segments.voice: Ramana's teaching survives in short works and in conversations his visitors wrote down. One small booklet carries the question as its title: in Tamil, Nan Yar, who am I? This is a paraphrase, not his words, but the method goes like this. Every thought you have is somebody's thought. Before the worry, before the plan, there is an I that has it. In Ramana's account, that sense of I is the first thought, and every other thought rises after it. So when a thought comes, don't follow it out into the world. Turn it around: to whom did this come? To me. And who am I? Not a riddle to solve with words. Ramana goes through the obvious answers: not the body, not the senses, not even the thinking mind. One way readers put it: each of these can be noticed, and the I is the one noticing. The point is to keep attention on the I itself, and trace it back toward where it rises. He gives a striking picture for what the question does. At a cremation, someone stirs the fire with a stick, keeping it burning. At the end, the stick goes into the fire too. The question works on all the other thoughts like that stick, he says, and in the end it burns up as well. Then the asking stops, and what remains is not another thought. Yesterday a room sang names. Today, a single word, I, followed home.
screen: `EVERY THOUGHT IS SOMEBODY'S.` · `TO WHOM DID THIS COME?` · `NOT THE BODY, NOT THE MIND.` · `THE STICK THAT STIRS THE FIRE.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Ask "who am I?" once, inside, slowly, and wait without answering in words; if an answer shows up anyway, a job, a name, a mood, ask: to whom did this come? Ask again with a longer silence, and a third time with the longest silence of all. You're not looking for a reply, only at where the question lands.
Who am I? Ramana Maharshi's self-enquiry: meet each thought by asking to whom it came, and follow the I back to its source. Today's word.
Your line: who am I. A question that isn't meant to end in an answer. See you tomorrow.

1398.title: The guru
1398.hook: Hindu paths give the teacher a weighty place, a relationship to approach with care
1398.howItsDone: In Hindu traditions that center on a guru, a student seeks out a teacher, often receives instruction or a mantra from them, learns through questions and service, and honors teachers on festivals such as Guru Purnima.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was who am I: Ramana Maharshi's question, followed rather than answered. Your line was who am I.

Who taught you to tie your shoes? Not a manual. Somebody knelt down, took the laces, went slowly, and let you get it wrong a few times. Some things travel well in books. Some, it seems, only travel hand to hand, from a person who can do them to a person who wants to. In the Upanishads, this kind of teaching is pictured that way: handed on by someone who has walked the road, to someone just starting out. That person has a name, now an English word worn thin by headlines about marketing and fitness.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU TO TIE YOUR SHOES?` → `HAND TO HAND, NOT BY MANUAL.` → `A WORD WORN THIN.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit, guru is a teacher, and as an ordinary adjective it also means heavy, weighty: someone whose words carry weight. A later text gives a traditional explanation that hears the syllables as darkness and its remover. It's a teaching more than a dictionary entry, but it shows how the role is felt. The Mundaka Upanishad gives the scene. A seeker who wants to know what is real should go to a teacher with fuel in hand, a small gift for the teacher's fire. And it names what to look for: a teacher learned in the sacred texts, and established in Brahman, the ultimate reality. Two tests, not one. Knowing the texts isn't enough. Living what they point to isn't either. The Bhagavad Gita adds the student's side. Learn it, Krishna tells Arjuna, by bowing, by asking questions, and by service; the wise who have seen the truth will teach you. Asking questions is right there in the verse. And the same texts that honor the teacher also warn. The Katha Upanishad describes people wise in their own eyes, going round and round, like the blind led by the blind. A guru is trusted with a great deal: a student's time, attention, hopes, sometimes a whole life. Trust that weighty is the point of the relationship, and it's exactly why it should be given slowly, with eyes open, and with both of the Mundaka's tests in mind.
screen: `GURU: WEIGHTY, A TEACHER.` · `FUEL IN HAND, TO ONE WHO KNOWS AND LIVES IT.` · `BOW, ASK, SERVE.` · `THE BLIND LED BY THE BLIND.` · then, large: `TRUST THAT WEIGHTY, GIVEN SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something that mattered, and ask what made their teaching land. Then picture a teacher for the deepest things you care about, name three qualities you'd look for, and set them beside the Mundaka's two: do they know the tradition, and do they live it? And one more, from the Gita: would they welcome your questions?
Guru. In Sanskrit, a teacher, and weighty: someone whose words carry weight, trusted to hand on what books can't. Today's word.
Your line: choose with care. Yesterday's teacher, Ramana, was such a figure for the people who came to his hill. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1399.title: The ambrosial hour
1399.hook: Sikhs rise before dawn for prayer and meditation
1399.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the amrit vela rise in the hours before dawn, bathe, and give the time to meditation on the Name and the morning prayers, at home or in the gurdwara, before the work of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was guru: a teacher whose words carry weight, and the two tests, do they know it, do they live it. Your line was choose with care.

An alarm goes off with nothing scheduled after it. No meeting, no shift, no school bell. Someone gets up anyway, washes, wraps a turban or covers their hair, and sits down on the floor with a small book, or walks to the gurdwara, where the doors are already open. Outside, the birds haven't started. The day hasn't asked for anything yet. That's the point. Today the path turns from Hindu ways to Sikh ways, and it starts before the sun.
screen: `AN ALARM, NOTHING SCHEDULED.` → `THE DOORS ARE ALREADY OPEN.` → `THE DAY HASN'T ASKED YET.`

segments.voice: Amrit vela: the ambrosial hour, the early hours before dawn. Amrit is nectar, the drink of immortality, and it's also the word Sikhs use for the sweetened water of initiation. Vela is the time, the hour. Put together: the nectar time. It comes right at the start of the Guru Granth Sahib, in Guru Nanak's Japji. The fourth stanza says, in paraphrase: in the ambrosial hours, meditate on the true Name, and reflect on God's greatness. Two jobs for the early hour: remember the Name, and consider how great is the one it names. A later Guru, Guru Ram Das, is even more practical. In a passage of the Guru Granth Sahib he describes someone who calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru. That person, he says, rises early and meditates on the Name, makes the effort in the early morning, bathes in the pool of nectar, and then goes on through the day singing the Guru's word. Notice the order. In the passage, the early hour isn't an escape from the day. It's the start of it, and the day is meant to carry what was found there. And why so early? The texts don't give a lecture on it. But the hour has its own texture. The phone hasn't buzzed. Nobody needs you. The mind hasn't filled up yet. Whatever you put in first, it seems, has room.
screen: `AMRIT VELA: THE NECTAR TIME.` · `JAPJI: THE NAME, AND GOD'S GREATNESS.` · `RISE EARLY, BATHE, REMEMBER.` · `THE START OF THE DAY, NOT AN ESCAPE.` · then, large: `WHAT GOES IN FIRST HAS ROOM.`

segments.voice: Sit as if it were that hour: dim a light if you can, settle, and notice what the room sounds like when it isn't asking for anything. If you pray, you can remember a name of God you hold dear; if you don't, just sit in the quiet.
Amrit vela. The ambrosial hour before dawn, when Sikhs who keep it rise to remember the Name before the day begins asking. Today's word.
Your line: the early hour. Before the phone, before the day's first ask, the doors are already open. See you tomorrow.

1400.title: Daily prayers
1400.hook: Sikhs recite set prayers morning, evening and night, beginning with Japji
1400.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep nitnem recite set prayers each day: Japji, Jaap Sahib and the Savaiye in the morning, Rehras in the evening, and Kirtan Sohila at night, often from a small prayer book called a gutka, and some add further prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was amrit vela: the ambrosial hour before dawn, kept for the Name. Your line was the early hour.

Open the book. It's a gutka, a pocket-sized collection of prayers, often wrapped in cloth and kept somewhere high and clean. The pages are worn at the front. That's where the morning starts. There's another worn place further in, for sunset, and one near the back, for bed. Three worn places in one small book: a day, in prayer, from first light to the last.
screen: `OPEN THE BOOK.` → `A GUTKA, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `THREE WORN PLACES.`

segments.voice: Nitnem is the daily rule of prayer: nit, daily, and nem, a rule. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, sets it out. In the morning, Japji, Jaap Sahib and the Savaiye. In the evening, Rehras. At night, before sleep, Kirtan Sohila. Some Sikhs add more, and the practice varies, but in the code the morning opens with Japji, Guru Nanak's words at the very start of the Guru Granth Sahib. After the Mool Mantar, the root statement of one creator, comes a short verse: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and, says Nanak, true it shall ever be. Then the first stanza does something surprising. It takes away the tools you'd expect. By thinking, it says, in paraphrase, you can't reach it, though you think a hundred thousand times. By keeping silent, you don't get silence, even if you stay absorbed deep within. Hunger isn't satisfied by piling up whole worlds. A hundred thousand clever tricks, and not one goes with you. Then the question: so how does one become true? How is the wall of falsehood broken? And the answer: by walking in the hukam, the divine will, written in from the start. So the first prayer of a Sikh day begins by putting down cleverness. This week ran from Patanjali's stilling of the mind, through japa, kirtan, Ramana's question and the teacher, to the early hour. Today a small book gathers a day of prayer into three set places.
screen: `NIT, DAILY. NEM, A RULE.` · `MORNING, EVENING, NIGHT.` · `JAPJI: TRUE NOW, TRUE EVER.` · `NOT BY THINKING, NOT BY CLEVERNESS.` · then, large: `WALK IN THE WILL.`

segments.voice: Hold Japji's first stanza in plain words, one line to a breath: not by thinking, so let one busy thought go; not by silence alone, so let the effort to be quiet go too; not by piling up, so let the wish for more go; not by cleverness. Then rest in the question the stanza asks: how does one become true? If you pray, you can rest in the Name; if not, just let the question be.
Nitnem. The Sikh daily rule of prayer: set prayers at morning, evening and night, opening the morning with Japji. Today's word.
Your line: the daily prayers. Morning, evening and night, from one small book. Until tomorrow.
